report.headline: Projected usage drops from 22.6% in the G League to 17.8% in the NBA, below league average, while the true-shooting projection is unreliable and should not be used to size scoring efficiency.

projection.text: Player A is projected to use 17.8% of NBA possessions, down from a 22.6% usage rate in the G League, landing below the league-average usage of 20.0%.

risks.text: The true-shooting projection of 53.5% is built on a model that is worse than simply assuming league-average efficiency (4.7% error both ways), so no efficiency conclusion should be drawn from it.

Projected usage of 17.8% falls noticeably below both the NBA average of 20.0% and the naive folk-rule estimate of 17.0%, while the z-preservation baseline of 22.9% shows how much larger the role would be if standing were fully preserved — the gap signals a real, not marginal, role reduction.
Playmaking indicators were modest in the source season: an assist rate of 7.8% and only 1.702 assists per 75 possessions, limiting the case for an expanded ball-handling role in the NBA.

The estimate rests on only 45 historical G League-to-NBA transitions, a thin base for a move where the usage slope (0.531) and true-shooting slope (0.801) already show only partial carryover of prior standing.

strengths.text: In the source season Player A produced 20.1 points and 9.9 rebounds per 75 possessions, a heavy statistical load for a 50-game, 1,480-minute sample.
Source-season true shooting was 58.7%, +0.52 standard deviations above the G League average, indicating efficient scoring on that usage.
The usage-rate model beats the trivial league-average baseline (3.3% mean absolute error versus 4.3%), so the usage projection is worth trusting for ranking purposes.

Player A already stood 0.54 standard deviations above the G League average in usage and 0.52 above average in true shooting, and players who make this move typically sit only 0.27 standard deviations above their own league, suggesting a stronger-than-typical mover.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage spans 12.5% to 23.0%, a 10.5-point range against a league usage standard deviation of 5.2%, so the model can only rank this player relative to peers, not pin down a single value; the true-shooting projection performs no better than simply guessing the league average (4.7% error both ways) and carries no real information.
